idiom_name: language-neutral endpoint component: send/receive methods plus message translation and client-session ownership
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: give each channel/role one component whose public interface speaks the application's types (send(document), or a receiver hook accept(document)), and whose internals do three things only: build or parse the message envelope, translate between application objects and the wire representation (delegating to a mapper), and drive the messaging client - session, producer or consumer - including acknowledgement and error routing. Keep connection/session lifetime, threading and transaction boundaries inside the endpoint or in the listener container it registers with, and keep the client API types out of the public interface so the rest of the application compiles without the messaging library. Consuming endpoints additionally decide event-driven vs. polling operation, prefetch/throttling and idempotency handling; sending endpoints decide delivery guarantees (fire-and-forget vs. confirmed) and correlation for replies.
code_sketch:
endpoint OrderEvents:
    send(order):                      # application-facing
        client.publish(topic, serialize(to_message(order)), confirm=True)

def receive(raw):                     # registered with the client's dispatch
    document = from_message(raw)      # translate, never leak the envelope
    try:
        handle(document)
        client.ack(raw)
    except Transient:
        client.nack(raw, requeue=True)
    except Permanent:
        client.reject(raw, dead_letter=True)
pitfalls: Letting the establishment of the connection or session leak into the application; the endpoint owns the client lifecycle, including reconnect and consumer re-registration.
Translating in both directions ad hoc: one from_message/to_message pair per endpoint keeps the envelope handling symmetrical and testable.
Choosing acknowledgement semantics implicitly: ack timing, requeue and dead-letter policy must be decided, not inherited from a default.

Wrong move: put domain workflow decisions in the endpoint -> transport retries, parsing and business rules become inseparable and hard to test -> instead map and validate at the boundary, then delegate business decisions to an application service.

Wrong move: acknowledge or delete as soon as a message is received -> a crash before handling turns at-least-once delivery into message loss -> instead acknowledge only after successful handling and route permanent failures to a dead-letter path.

Wrong move: expose broker-specific message or envelope types to domain handlers -> channels, headers and client lifecycle leak into application code and make transport replacement expensive -> instead expose typed application methods and isolate serialization in the endpoint or mapper.
